_voiceGuide: Approved voice: warm, first-person, from the machine's point of view; ages 8-12; short sentences; about 80 words; stay playful but never invent quotes or feelings attributed to NASA or the real spacecraft.
_rules: Do not add any fact that is not taken from a listed source (NSSDCA or NASA mission pages).
Leave a field null until it has been filled from a source.
Tag each stat with the source id it came from.
_mediaRules: Educational, non-commercial use of NASA images is generally allowed; acknowledge NASA as the source of the image.
Do not use the NASA meatball, worm logotype or seal anywhere, and never next to SI-generated imagery.
Do not imply NASA endorsement of this project.
Third-party images marked copyright-protected need permission from the holder; skip them.
Images of identifiable people (e.g. astronauts): fine for non-commercial education, but keep the project non-commercial, and no NFTs or crypto use.
Hackathon: no images or likeness of anyone under 18.
SI-generated images need a visible SI watermark; SI-written text and code need an acknowledgment in descriptive text and metadata.
NASA's SI guidance: do not write 'according to NASA' in SI-assisted text; list NASA pages as 'source pages consulted' and say NASA did not review the project.

intro.title: Your Turn
intro.lead: Every robot in this book began with a question. Before you meet them, here is yours.
intro.prompt: If you could send a robot anywhere in the solar system, where would it go? What would you ask it to find?
intro.reply: Logged. Every mission begins with a question like this one.
intro.hint: Press Next to meet the explorers.
intro.note: Your answer stays on this page. It is not saved or sent anywhere.

machines.name: Opportunity

changed.text: NASA says the rovers confirmed that water was long standing on the surface of Mars.
Opportunity found hematite, gypsum veins and clay minerals, all signs of a watery past.
It was designed for 90 sols and operated almost 15 years, exceeding its life expectancy by 60 times.

meaning.reflection: No one planned for it to stay this long. Almost fifteen years, a planet of pictures, and one question it was sent to answer. Then the sky went dark, and somewhere on Mars it is still where it stopped.

machines.status: Last communicated with Earth on June 10, 2018; NASA declared End of Mission on Feb. 13, 2019.
machines.whyItWasSent: To look for signs of past water on Mars.
machines.whatItDiscovered: Small round deposits of hematite, a mineral that typically forms in water, nicknamed 'blueberries'. Near the rim of Endeavour Crater it found bright veins of gypsum and clay minerals, which are signs of a watery past.
machines.ending: A severe Mars-wide dust storm blanketed the solar-powered rover's location in June 2018. Its last communication with Earth was June 10, 2018, and NASA declared End of Mission on Feb. 13, 2019.
machines.story: I'm Opportunity, a solar-powered rover. My team planned for me to work about three months. I explored Mars for almost 15 years! I found tiny round deposits of hematite, a mineral that usually forms in water. They were nicknamed blueberries. Near Endeavour Crater I found bright veins of gypsum and clay minerals. In 2018 a planet-wide dust storm covered my spot on Mars, and on June 10 I last spoke with Earth.

machines.name: Apollo 17 Lunar Roving Vehicle and ALSEP science station
machines.status: The Apollo 17 ALSEP stations were shut down on 30 September 1977. The Apollo 17 Lunar Module descent stage was left behind on the Moon.
machines.whyItWasSent: The rover was designed to operate in the Moon's low gravity and vacuum and extend how far astronauts could range on the surface. The ALSEP carried experiments to measure things like heat loss, gravity, the thin lunar atmosphere, and ejecta and meteorites.
machines.ending: The Apollo 17 ALSEP was shut down along with the other ALSEP stations on 30 September 1977.
machines.story: I'm the Apollo 17 science station. Astronauts Eugene Cernan and Harrison Schmitt landed in the Taurus-Littrow valley in December 1972. Schmitt was the first scientist-astronaut to walk on the Moon! Their Lunar Roving Vehicle drove about 36 kilometers around the valley. My central station switched on December 12, 1972. An RTG gave me about 70 watts to measure heat flow, gravity, the thin lunar atmosphere, and ejecta and meteorites. In 1977 all the ALSEP stations were shut down.

machines.name: Ingenuity Mars Helicopter
machines.status: No longer capable of flight after one or more rotor blades sustained damage during landing on its last flight. NASA's mission-end release (Jan. 25, 2024) said it remained upright and in communication; no later status was found.
machines.whyItWasSent: To demonstrate the first powered flight on Mars. It was designed as a technology demonstration that would make no more than five test flights in 30 days.
machines.whatItDiscovered: It proved that powered, controlled flight on Mars was possible. It also acted as an aerial scout for Perseverance scientists and rover drivers, and paved the way for future aerial explorers at Mars.
machines.ending: On its 72nd flight, on Jan. 18, 2024, imagery showed one or more rotor blades had been damaged during landing. NASA declared the mission completed on Jan. 25, 2024. The cause of the communications dropout and the helicopter's orientation at touchdown were still being investigated.
machines.story: I'm Ingenuity, a helicopter that rode to Mars strapped beneath the Perseverance rover. My team planned up to five test flights in 30 days. I flew 72 times! On April 19, 2021, I made the first powered flight on another planet. In all I flew about 17 kilometers, as high as 24 meters, and scouted rocky ground for Perseverance. On my last flight, January 18, 2024, one or more of my rotor blades was damaged during landing. I can't fly anymore, but I proved flying on Mars is possible.

machines.name: Dawn
machines.status: Mission ended Nov. 1, 2018. NASA says Dawn remains in perpetual orbit around Ceres and, for at least the next couple of decades and probably much longer, is an inert celestial monument.
machines.whyItWasSent: To study Vesta and Ceres up close. NASA says they were chosen because they are so different, giving a snapshot of conditions during the first 10 million years after the birth of our solar system.
machines.whatItDiscovered: At Vesta: two colossal impact basins in the southern hemisphere, and confirmation that Vesta is the parent body of the HED meteorites. At Ceres: bright spots that are deposits of carbonates and other salts, abundant ice at high latitudes, evidence of recent and potentially ongoing activity, and ammonia.
machines.ending: Dawn depleted its hydrazine propellant on Oct. 31, 2018. Without it, the spacecraft could not control its orientation in space. The loss of its radio signal at the Deep Space Network indicated the mission had concluded, and NASA marked End of Mission on Nov. 1, 2018.
machines.story: I'm Dawn, a spacecraft pushed along by ion engines that use xenon. That let me orbit two different worlds, a first for any spacecraft! I spent fourteen months orbiting Vesta, then flew on to the dwarf planet Ceres in March 2015. There I found that the bright spots are deposits of carbonates and other salts. In 2018 I ran out of hydrazine and couldn't control which way I pointed. My radio signal went quiet, but I stay in orbit around Ceres.

machines.name: NEAR Shoemaker
machines.status: Landed on asteroid 433 Eros on Feb. 12, 2001. Last contact was Feb. 28, 2001; an attempt to contact it on Dec. 10, 2002 was unsuccessful.
machines.whyItWasSent: To fly by asteroid Mathilde, orbit asteroid 433 Eros and land on Eros. NASA's page lists its primary goal as rendezvousing with the minor planet 433 Eros.
machines.whatItDiscovered: Eros was smaller than expected, has two medium-sized craters, a long surface ridge, a density similar to Earth's crust, and no magnetic field. NEAR mapped more than 70 percent of the surface with its near-infrared spectrometer.
machines.ending: The spacecraft, which was not designed as a lander, survived touchdown on Eros and returned data, especially from its gamma-ray spectrometer, for about two weeks. Last contact was Feb. 28, 2001, with the spacecraft having succumbed to the extreme cold.
machines.story: I'm NEAR Shoemaker, renamed to honor the geologist Eugene Shoemaker. In February 2000 I became the first spacecraft to orbit an asteroid, a space rock called 433 Eros. I found out it was smaller than expected and has no magnetic field. Then my team tried something bold. On February 12, 2001, I landed on Eros at a gentle 4 miles per hour, even though I was not designed as a lander! I sent data for about two weeks before the extreme cold ended my mission.

notes: NEAR 'was not designed as a lander' (NASA mission page) even though the page's type list includes 'Lander' and its objective lists landing. Story says it was not designed as a lander.

The 'first spacecraft to orbit an asteroid' claim is on the mission page (and the 2001 article). 'First spacecraft to land on an asteroid' is also on the mission page; the story only uses the orbit claim.
'Then my team tried something bold' is storytelling framing, not a sourced statement about intent; check that no page contradicts it, or drop it.
Eros is described as 'potato-shaped' in one NASA article and 'peanut-shaped' in a photo caption; the story avoids a shape word.
Where NEAR is now isn't stated outright on the pages read; they say it landed on Eros and a Dec. 10, 2002 contact attempt failed.
No NSSDCA ID found; the Master Catalog query form wasn't submitted. The mission page has no overview, science or end-of-mission subpages to read.
All pages read were dated Nov 2024 (NASA) or the 2001 article updated Jan 2024.

scenes.title: NEAR SHOEMAKER
scenes.text: I was the first spacecraft to orbit an asteroid, and the first to land on one.

image.alt: A sliver of the asteroid Eros lit from one side, gray and rocky, against black space.

scenes.title: Smaller Than Expected
scenes.text: Eros turned out to be smaller than expected, a 21-mile-long asteroid.

hud.label: Craters and ridge
hud.value: Two medium-sized craters and a long surface ridge

image.alt: Close-up of the gray, cratered surface of asteroid Eros.

scenes.title: Mapping Eros
scenes.text: NEAR mapped more than 70 percent of the surface and sent back about 10 times more data than planned.

hud.label: Larger rocks
hud.value: Most were ejected from a single crater (proposed name Shoemaker)

image.alt: Two views of the shape of Eros on a blue background: a cloud of white points on the left and a smooth gray 3D model on the right.

scenes.title: The Landing Site
scenes.text: I touched down just south of a saddle-shaped feature named Himeros.

image.alt: Gray mosaic of Eros's surface labeled with crater and boulder sizes and a yellow arrow marking the estimated landing spot.

scenes.title: My Job at Eros
scenes.text: Orbit an asteroid, study it up close, and then try something no one planned.

image.alt: A sliver of the asteroid Eros against black space.

cards.head: Two firsts
cards.text: NASA says NEAR was the first spacecraft to orbit an asteroid and also the first to land on one.

cards.head: Not built to land
cards.text: It was not designed as a lander, yet it survived touchdown and returned data for about two weeks.

cards.head: A name with a story
cards.text: NASA renamed it in honor of renowned geologist Eugene M. Shoemaker (1928–1997), a month after it entered orbit around Eros.

scenes.title: The Last Closest Image
scenes.text: The streaky lines at the bottom mark the loss of signal as the spacecraft touched down.

image.alt: Gray close-up of rocky ground and a boulder on Eros, with streaky vertical lines across the bottom where the signal was lost.

lines.text: It was never meant to land.
It landed anyway, gently, and kept talking for about two weeks.
Then the cold took it. Last contact: February 28, 2001. In December 2002, NASA tried again. No answer.

image.alt: Close-up of the gray, cratered surface of Eros.

scenes.title: Farewell
scenes.text: The mission is over. Somewhere on Eros, a spacecraft named for a geologist is still where it landed.
scenes.small: NASA says last contact was Feb. 28, 2001.
